objectives: Name the Five Great Messengers.
Explain what the title Ulul-Azm means.
Say what their mission was.
Use to + verb for purpose.
content.pedagogy: The opening chapter introduces the Five Great Messengers and the idea of patience. A simple list of the five names with the honorifics helps learners read the names with respect.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Ulul-Azm is a title for five prophets; it is not the name of one prophet.
Their mission was to guide people, not to rule them.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: to + verb (purpose) · was / were + adjective
Look (Activity 1): a mission … to guide people.
Practise (Activity 2): fill patient, stay and promise.
Likely errors: *for guide people · *They was patient.
Use (Activity 3): being patient.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: U-lul AZM, NO-ah, A-bra-ham, MO-ses, JE-sus, mu-HAM-mad.
Stress: PA-tient, MIS-sion, MA-jor.
beforeReading: Ask: “What does it mean to be patient?”
duringReading: First reading: Who are the Five Great Messengers?
Second reading: list the five names.
Find what the title means.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–16 List the names; 16–20 Quick Challenge; 20–32 Language Focus 1–2; 32–38 Use: being patient; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why do you think patience was important for the prophets?
What did the messengers invite people to do?
What did Allah promise?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Ulul-Azm” and “A Mission” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: patient, mission, true path, stay away, major.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the list of the five names.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write four sentences about the Five Great Messengers with to + verb.

expectedResponses: Allah chose five leader prophets. Their title means they were very patient and had a strong character. They had a mission to guide people to Allah’s true path.
content.transferTask: Write about a time you were patient.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners read the names with the honorifics?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “to + verb” about the messengers.

objectives: Explain how idol worship began among Noah’s people.
Put the events in order.
Name the five good men.
Use first, later and then.
content.pedagogy: The chapter explains step by step how respect for good people slowly turned into idol worship. A step chart (good men → pictures → statues → worship) helps learners see how a small change grew over many years.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The five men were good people who prayed to Allah; they were not idols at first.
People first made pictures and statues only to remember them, not to worship them.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: first · later · then · after some time · past simple
Look (Activity 1): they first made pictures … Later, …
Practise (Activity 2): choose first, then and After.
Likely errors: *At the first · *After some times.
Use (Activity 3): remembering good people.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: WAD, su-WA’, ya-GHUS, ya-’UK, NASR, ibn AB-bas.
Stress: CEN-tu-ries, STAT-ues, re-SPECT.
beforeReading: Ask: “How do we remember good people who died?”
duringReading: First reading: How did idol worship begin?
Second reading: complete the step chart.
Find the five names.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–17 Step chart; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–32 Language Focus 1–2; 32–38 Use: remembering good people; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why did people make pictures of the good men?
What changed when people forgot the history?
Why did Allah send Noah?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Ten Centuries” and “Five Good Men” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: reported, in their minds, made pictures, figures, bowed down, prayed to.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the step chart with the first step written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write the story in five sentences with first, later and then.

expectedResponses: First, people made pictures of five good men. Later, they made statues of them. Then, people forgot the history and worshipped the statues, so Allah chose Noah as His messenger.
content.transferTask: Write about a good person you remember.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners see how the change happened step by step?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “first” and one with “later”.

objectives: Describe Noah’s character.
Explain the two paths people chose.
Explain why the rich leaders refused.
Use because and so that.
content.pedagogy: The chapter shows two groups: the poor and weak who believed, and the rich and powerful who refused. A two-column chart helps learners compare the groups and their reasons. The message of equality connects with learners’ own lives.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The rich leaders refused because of pride and power, not because the message was unclear.
Noah agreed that he was a human; a messenger needs to be a normal person so that people understand him.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: because (reason) · so that (purpose) · never
Look (Activity 1): … so that people can understand him easily.
Practise (Activity 2): choose because and never.
Likely errors: *so that people understands · *because of they wanted.
Use (Activity 3): everyone is equal.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: NO-ah, A-dam, ID-ris.
Stress: CAR-pen-ter, MES-sen-ger, PUN-ish-ment.
beforeReading: Ask: “Are rich people more important than poor people?”
duringReading: First reading: Who believed Noah?
Second reading: complete the two-column chart.
Find what the rich leaders asked Noah to do.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–18 Two-column chart; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–32 Language Focus 1–2; 32–38 Use: everyone is equal; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why did the poor people believe Noah?
Why did the rich leaders refuse?
Why did Noah not send away the poor believers?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “A Carpenter” and “Two Paths” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: brave, smart, punishment, Messenger, paths, argue with, liar, instead, make a deal with, belief, send away, respected.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chart with the headings: believed / refused.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short dialogue between Noah and a rich leader.

expectedResponses: Noah was brave, kind and honest. The poor and weak people believed him because believers are equal. The rich leaders refused because they wanted to protect their power.
content.transferTask: Write about why all people are equal.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners link the story with equality today?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “because” about the story.

content.chapter: Chapter 4: Nine Hundred and Fifty Years
objectives: Describe how Noah’s people answered his message.
Explain how Noah showed patience for 950 years.
Explain Noah’s prayer at the end.
Use kept + -ing, continued to and never.
content.pedagogy: The chapter shows great patience over a very long time. A timeline of the people’s answers (covered their ears → laughed → made fun → became cruel) shows how things got worse, while Noah stayed patient and kind.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Noah did not want anything for himself; he warned his people with a sad but honest heart.
Noah prayed only after Allah told him that no more people would believe.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: keep + -ing · continue to + verb · never · make fun of
Look (Activity 1): Noah kept talking to his people.
Practise (Activity 2): choose telling, to teach and never.
Likely errors: *kept tell · *continued teach.
Use (Activity 3): I did not give up.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Stress: MIS-sion, CRU-el, AR-gu-ment.
Numbers: nine hundred and fifty.
beforeReading: Ask: “What do you do when something is very difficult?”
duringReading: First reading: How did the people answer Noah?
Second reading: complete the timeline of their answers.
Find Noah’s prayer.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–16 Timeline; 16–20 Quick Challenge; 20–32 Language Focus 1–2; 32–38 Use: I did not give up; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why did the people cover their ears?
How did Noah show patience?
Why did Noah pray at the end?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “950 Years” and “Covered Ears” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: gave up, the truth, change their mind, laughed at, made fun of, cruel, beat, almost, on earth, accepted.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the timeline with the first answer written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write four sentences about Noah’s patience with kept and continued.

expectedResponses: Noah kept talking to his people and continued to teach them for 950 years. They laughed at him and became cruel, but he never gave up.
content.transferTask: Write about something you kept trying to do.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners see the contrast between the people and Noah?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “kept + -ing” about Noah.

objectives: Retell the story of the ark in order.
Explain why the people laughed at Noah.
Explain what happened to Noah’s son.
Use far from, except and were going to.
content.pedagogy: The longest and most dramatic chapter. A story map (build → laugh → water → go in → waves → the son) keeps the events clear. Read the part about Noah’s son calmly and keep to the words of the book.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Noah built the ship far from the sea because Allah showed him where to build it.
Noah’s wife and son did not believe, so they did not join the believers.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: far from · except · safe from · was / were going to
Look (Activity 1): they were going to see Allah’s great miracle.
Practise (Activity 2): choose from, except and from.
Likely errors: *far of the sea · *safe of the rain.
Use (Activity 3): doing the right thing.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Stress: MIR-a-cle, UN-be-liev-ers, IN-sect.
Sound: ark /ɑːrk/, flood /flʌd/.
beforeReading: Ask: “What would people think if someone built a big ship far from the sea?”
duringReading: First reading: Why did Noah build the ark?
Second reading: complete the story map.
Find what Noah said to his son.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–18 Story map; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–32 Language Focus 1–2; 32–38 Use: doing the right thing; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why did the people laugh at Noah?
Why did the ark become a safe home?
What did Noah say to his son?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Far from the Sea” and “Two of Every Animal” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: an ark, nails, look ready, quietly, Unbelievers, inside, safe from, pushed up, run up, drowned.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the story map with the first event written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Retell the chapter in six sentences from the point of view of a believer on the ark.

formativeAssessment: Uses far from or except correctly.
expectedResponses: Noah built an ark far from the sea, and the people laughed at him. When the water came, the believers and the animals went into the ark. The Ark kept them safe from the heavy rain.
content.transferTask: Write about doing the right thing when others laugh.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners read the part about Noah’s son calmly?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “far from” and one with “except”.

objectives: Describe how the flood ended.
Say where the ship landed.
Say what Noah did after he left the ark.
Understand imperatives.
content.pedagogy: A short, calm chapter after the drama of the flood. It ends with thankfulness: Noah puts his head on the ground to thank Allah. Learners connect this with their own ways of saying thank you.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The ship landed on Mount Judi, not on the sea shore.
Noah let the animals go; he did not keep them.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: imperatives · let + base verb · to + verb (purpose)
Look (Activity 1): Earth, take the water back! Sky, stop the rain!
Practise (Activity 2): choose landed, go and to thank.
Likely errors: *let them to go · *for thank Allah.
Use (Activity 3): saying thank you.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: MOUNT ju-DI.
Intonation: commands fall at the end: “Stop the RAIN!”
beforeReading: Ask: “How do you feel after a big storm ends?”
duringReading: First reading: How did the flood end?
Second reading: underline the commands.
Find what Noah did after he left the ark.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–9 First reading; 9–14 Commands; 14–18 Quick Challenge; 18–32 Language Focus 1–2; 32–38 Use: saying thank you; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What happened to the water?
Why did Noah let the animals go?
Why did Noah thank Allah?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Mount Judi” and “All Over the Earth” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: the ground.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the frame: Noah put his head on the ground to …
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write four sentences about the end of the flood.

formativeAssessment: Uses let or to + verb correctly.
expectedResponses: Allah said, “Earth, take the water back! Sky, stop the rain!” The ship landed on Mount Judi. Noah let the animals go and put his head on the ground to thank Allah.
content.transferTask: Write about a time you felt very thankful.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners connect the story with thankfulness?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “let” and one with “to thank”.

objectives: Explain Noah’s two pieces of advice.
Explain why believing in Allah is more important than everything.
Say why people still remember his story.
Use told them (not) to and more important than.
content.pedagogy: The closing chapter gives Noah’s last advice to his children. Learners report the advice with “told them (not) to” and then build a class poster of lessons from the whole book. The poster shows only the ark, never the prophet.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Noah gave two pieces of advice: believe only in Allah, and never be arrogant.
“Arrogant” means thinking you are better than others.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: tell someone (not / never) to + verb · more important than
Look (Activity 1): He told them to believe only in Allah.
Practise (Activity 2): choose told, to be and than.
Likely errors: *He said them to · *never be arrogant (after told).
Use (Activity 3): advice I got.
beforeReading: Ask: “What is the best advice an older person gave you?”
duringReading: First reading: What advice did Noah give?
Second reading: write the two pieces of advice.
Find why people still remember his story.
afterReading: Group task: “Our Ark of Good Advice”.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–9 First reading; 9–14 Two pieces of advice; 14–18 Quick Challenge; 18–32 Language Focus 1–2; 32–38 Use: advice I got; 38–40 Exit ticket. (Poster in a second lesson.)
discussionPoints: Why did Noah give advice before he died?
Why is it important not to be arrogant?
What can we learn from Noah’s story today?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Last Advice” and “Today” when the picture is in place.
The group task “Our Ark of Good Advice” closes the book.
Do not draw prophets or people on the poster; draw only the ark, the water and the animals.
Word Notes: arrogant.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the frame: He told them to … / He told them never to …
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short letter from Noah’s child about the advice.

formativeAssessment: Explains the two pieces of advice.
Says why people remember the story.
expectedResponses: Before he died, Noah told his children to believe only in Allah and never to pray to other gods. He also told them never to be arrogant.
content.transferTask: Write about good advice you got from an older person.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners report the advice correctly?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “He told them to …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains the two pieces of advice.
Says why people remember the story.

metadata.title: Noah A2 — Teacher’s Book
metadata.subtitle: Prophet Noah (pbuh)
metadata.estimatedDuration: 7 chapter units of 40 minutes each. Whole-book review pages follow separately.
metadata.targetLearners: Young learners and adults who can read short, simple texts about people, events and values, and who can write short connected sentences.
metadata.purpose: Develop A2 reading, listening, speaking and writing through the story of Prophet Noah: the Five Great Messengers, how idol worship began, Noah’s patient call, the ark, the flood and his last advice, using the Language Focus attached to every story chapter.
metadata.approachDesc: Every story chapter follows the TYMM route. YDAB1 listening and YDAB2 reading establish meaning; the Quick Challenge checks comprehension. Grammar is then learned in small steps: in the Language Focus, learners first LOOK at a form in a real chapter sentence, then PRACTISE it in controlled, meaningful tasks, and finally USE it in short YDAB3 speaking and YDAB4 writing about their own world.
metadata.assessmentEvidence: 7 Quick Challenges, text-evidence checks, chapter Language Focus tasks (Look → Practise → Use), exit tickets, Knowledge Check, Vocabulary Challenge, Language Review and Final Challenge.

formative: Short spoken and written Use tasks

readingFramework.before: Activate only what the chapter needs: a short question, a picture of the sea or a ship, or a word from daily life.
readingFramework.during: Listen first for gist (when the audio is ready), then read and follow the chapter’s own structure: a list of names, steps in order, two groups or a story in order.
readingFramework.after: Complete the Quick Challenge, then the chapter’s Language Focus (look → practise → use), then a short production about the learners’ own world.

vocabularyApproach.selection: Word Notes are the bold words of the teacher-approved text. Prioritize them and the words needed for the chapter’s key idea.
vocabularyApproach.method: Infer meaning from context or a picture before any direct explanation.
vocabularyApproach.recycling: Reuse vocabulary in Language Focus tasks, exit tickets and the Language Review.

metadata.grammarApproach: Text-based and in small steps. Start from the story sentence, ask a simple meaning question (What does this word show?), let learners answer, then confirm the rule and practice it in context. Rule explanations appear in the app only after learners answer.
grammarSequence: Ch1: to + verb (purpose) · was / were + adjective
Ch2: first · later · then · after some time · past simple
Ch4: keep + -ing · continue to + verb · never · make fun of
Ch5: far from · except · safe from · was / were going to
Ch6: imperatives · let + base verb · to + verb (purpose)
Ch7: tell someone (not / never) to + verb · more important than

skillsFocus.listening: TYMM YDAB1: follow narration for gist, people and key events.
skillsFocus.reading: TYMM YDAB2: find key information, put events in order and understand simple reasons.
skillsFocus.speaking: TYMM YDAB3: describe people, events and good actions in short connected sentences.
skillsFocus.writing: TYMM YDAB4: write short connected sentences with and, but, so and because.

valuesFocus: D12 Patience — Waiting calmly and not giving up.
D1 Justice — Treating all people as equal.
D10 Humility — Not thinking that you are better than others.
D6 Honesty — Always telling the truth.
languageFocus: Every one of the 7 chapters has a Language Focus set built as Look → Practise → Use (3 activities).
Use the Language Focus after basic comprehension and the Quick Challenge.
Always start from the story sentence and ask a meaning question before naming the form.
The Use step is connected spoken or written production about a new, non-story situation.
metadata.differentiationNotes: Reduce linguistic load without lowering the thinking target: one paragraph at a time, charts given in part, picture cards, audio replay, sentence frames and oral rehearsal. Extend by asking for one more sentence or one more reason from the book, not by introducing outside facts.

sensitiveNotes.title: Source fidelity and respectful teaching
notes: Keep explanations within the wording of the book; do not add outside details or opinions.
Never draw or act out Prophet Noah or any prophet. Posters and pictures show only the ark, the water, the land and the animals.
The Qur’an quotations and the hadith belong to the teacher-approved text; they are read as they are, without extra comment.
Read the parts about the punishment and about Noah’s son calmly, in the words of the book.

globalCitizenship.title: Global Citizenship and Cultural Bridges
globalCitizenship.description: The story of Prophet Noah connects with questions every community faces today: how to treat rich and poor people equally, how to stay patient and how to be thankful.

themes.title: Equal dignity:
themes.description: Noah would never send away the poor and weak believers (Chapter 3). Discuss how communities can treat everyone as equal.

themes.title: Patience and hope:
themes.description: Noah taught his people for 950 years and never gave up (Chapter 4). Discuss why patience matters when change is slow.

themes.title: Caring for living things:
themes.description: Allah told Noah to take two of every animal and insect (Chapter 5). Discuss how people can protect animals today.

actions: Ask an older family member for one piece of good advice and write it down.
Find Mount Judi on a modern map.
Make a small poster about patience for your classroom.

exitTicket: One thing I learned about Prophet Noah today is …
One new word from today’s chapter is …
One good action I can do this week is …

miniProject.title: Our Ark of Good Advice
miniProject.desc: In groups, draw a big ark (no people), choose four lessons from the book, write each on a card and present one card to the class.

reflectivePrompt.title: A Lesson from Noah
reflectivePrompt.desc: Noah taught his people for 950 years and never gave up (Chapter 4). Write four to five sentences about one lesson from his story and how you can follow it.

valuesEducation.title: TYMM Values in Action
valuesEducation.description: Use only values the chapter really shows. Ask for the sentence first, then connect the value to a small action learners can do and see. See https://tymm.meb.gov.tr/beceriler/erdem-deger-eylem-cercevesi.

items.label: D12 Patience
items.value: Patience: Noah taught his people for 950 years and never gave up (Chapter 4).

items.label: D1 Justice
items.value: Justice: Noah would never send away the poor and weak believers, because believers are equal (Chapter 3).

items.label: D10 Humility
items.value: Humility: Noah told his children never to be arrogant (Chapter 7).

items.label: D6 Honesty
items.value: Honesty: Noah was kind, honest and patient, and he always told the truth (Chapter 3).

questions: What small action can show it this week?
Which part is from the book and which part is my own idea?

cefrProfile.intro: This book is written for CEFR A2. The table links the A2 descriptors of the End-of-Level Test A2 to the chapters of this book where learners practice them.

rows.descriptor: Can understand short, simple texts containing the highest frequency vocabulary, including a proportion of shared international vocabulary items.
practice: Chapter 5 (The Ark): Put the events of the story in order.
Whole book: Knowledge Check and Final Challenge.

rows.descriptor: Can write a series of simple phrases and sentences linked with simple connectors like “and”, “but” and “because”.
practice: Chapter 4 (Nine Hundred and Fifty Years): Write about something you kept trying to do.
Language Review, “Use: A Lesson from Noah”: Write four to five sentences.

rows.descriptor: Can give a simple description or presentation of people, living or working conditions, daily routines, likes/dislikes, etc. as a short series of simple phrases and sentences linked into a list.
practice: Chapter 6 (The Flood Ends): Talk about a time you felt very thankful.
Chapter 7 (Noah’s Last Advice): Present one card from the class ark.

test.title: End-of-Level Test A2
test.when: Give the test when the class has finished the A2 books it reads this term. It has four parts and takes about 60 minutes plus a short speaking test for each learner.
parts: Reading and Language (40 minutes): in the app. The learner gets a test code at the end.
Writing (20 minutes): on paper. Write an email to a friend about a visit to an old place. (50–70 words)
Speaking (about 6 minutes): one learner with the teacher, in 2 parts.
Scoring: type the test code in “Score a test”, then score Writing and Speaking with the bands. Copy the pilot line for the pilot results sheet.

content.grammarFocus: Look at “Noah kept talking to his people”: again and again. Then choose telling, to teach and never.

content.lessonPlan: What do you do when something is difficult? Write one idea. Read the chapter and find how the people answered. Make a timeline of their answers.

whatToNotice: Noah taught his people for a very long time.
readListen: What do you do when something is difficult? Write one idea.

metadata.title: Noah A2 — Self-Study Guide
metadata.subtitle: Read • Find • Check • Build • Use
metadata.estimatedStudyTime: About 20 minutes per chapter, plus the review pages at the end
metadata.whoIsThisFor: A2 learners who read the story of Prophet Noah alone or with a teacher.
learningGoals: Find evidence in the text before answering.
Understand the story of Prophet Noah, the ark and the flood.
Explain the lessons of patience, equality and humility in the story.
Use each chapter’s Language Focus in connected sentences.
recommendedUse: Study one chapter at a time.
Read (and listen, when the audio is ready) before the Quick Challenge.
Repair wrong answers with the text.
Do the Language Focus after you understand the chapter.
Do the review pages after Chapter 7.

readingDiary.intro: Keep this diary when you finish the book. Write short answers.
prompts: The date I finished the book:
My favorite chapter, and one reason:
One thing from the story of Prophet Noah that I liked:
One sentence for a friend: “Read this book because …”
One new word I want to keep:
The next book I want to read in the library:

sections.title: 1. Make Your Plan
sections.text: This book has 7 chapters. Plan the whole book before Chapter 1.
points: Choose your study days and how many chapters you will read each week.
Write one personal goal for this book.
Save new words to My words and review them after one day, three days and one week.

sections.title: 2. One Chapter per Session
sections.text: Each chapter takes about 20 minutes. Open “Study Path” for the steps of your chapter.
points: Preview the title and the “Before You Read” question.
Read for the main idea.
Find the evidence.
Do the Quick Challenge.
Do the Language Focus.

sections.title: 3. Read and Listen
sections.text: Read every chapter twice: once for the main idea, once for the details. When the audio is ready, listen once while you follow the text.
points: First reading: What is the chapter about?
Second reading: Mark names, dates and linking words.
Say one long sentence aloud with the right pauses.

sections.title: 4. Word Notes
sections.text: Bold words have Word Notes. Use them after you have tried to understand the sentence yourself.
points: Guess the meaning from the sentence.
Check the Word Note.
Write the word in a new sentence of your own.

sections.title: 5. Quick Challenge
sections.text: Answer before you read the feedback. If you are wrong, repair the answer with the text.
points: Find the paragraph the question is about.
Read the key sentence again.
Explain why the right answer is right, then try again.

sections.title: 6. Language Focus
sections.text: Each chapter has 3 Language Focus activities built from the chapter’s own sentences.
points: Activity 1 (Notice): Look at a sentence and what it means.
Activities 2–3 (Build): Choose, complete, correct or rewrite forms.
Activity 4 (Use): Write or say connected sentences about a different situation.

sections.title: 7. When It Is Hard
sections.text: Some chapters have many names and dates. Change how you study, not your goal.
points: Read one paragraph only.
Make a time line of the dates.
List the names and what each one did.
Learn only three words today.

sections.title: 8. Values in the Book
sections.text: The book shows patience, justice, humility and honesty. Find the sentence first, then think of a small action of your own.
points: Patience: Patience: Noah taught his people for 950 years and never gave up (Chapter 4).
Justice: Justice: Noah would never send away the poor and weak believers, because believers are equal (Chapter 3).
Humility: Humility: Noah told his children never to be arrogant (Chapter 7).
Honesty: Honesty: Noah was kind, honest and patient, and he always told the truth (Chapter 3).

sections.title: 9. At the End of the Book
sections.text: After Chapter 7, do the review pages in this order. Go back to a chapter when an answer is not clear.
points: Knowledge Check
Vocabulary Challenge
Master Glossary
Language Review
Final Challenge

sections.title: 10. Look Back
sections.text: Before Chapter 1 and again at the end, answer the “I can” statements of a few chapters. What can you do now that you could not do before?
points: Which chapter changed what you knew?
Tell the story of the ark to someone at home in four sentences, in your home language or in English.
